issues.legal_issue: An award that merely records a partition already completed does not, on that account, require registration as an instrument creating or declaring rights in immovable property.
material_facts: The family’s immovable properties had been partitioned before the award was made, and the parties had taken separate possession and enjoyment of their allotted properties.
A later arbitration agreement recorded that the partition had already occurred and that a party who had previously been a minor accepted it.
The award referred to the completed partition and the parties’ possession under it; it did not itself effect that partition.
issues.conclusion: The award’s reference to the prior partition did not make it compulsorily registrable as an instrument creating or declaring interests in immovable property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a non-testamentary instrument that creates or declares rights or interests in immovable property of the specified value requires registration. A recital of an existing partition does not itself create or declare those rights. The Court relied on Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Bhaskarsa Kabadi.

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: A party sought to have an arbitration award filed and enforced, and the opposing party contested its admissibility.
predicates.partition_previously_completed: The parties had already divided the immovable property and taken possession of their respective shares before the award was made.
predicates.award_only_recites_partition: The award referred to the earlier division and possession but did not itself carry out the division.

issues.definition: When an award is sought to be enforced after the property has already been divided, a reference in the award only to that completed division means the award is not registrable on the ground that it effected the partition.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered charge in an award does not prevent the award from being admitted to prove a severable, independently existing personal obligation to pay money.
material_facts: The arbitrators found that two family members had received more than their shares from family funds and directed them to pay the amounts due to the other family members.
The award made the payors personally liable and also created a charge over their immovable properties to secure payment.
The personal payment obligation existed independently of the charge; the charge added a means of recovering the debt from the properties.
The charge was created for the first time by the award and was not registered.
issues.conclusion: The unregistered charge could not affect the immovable properties or be admitted as evidence of the charge, but the award was admissible to establish the severable personal obligation to pay.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act bars an unregistered document that requires registration from affecting the immovable property or being received as evidence of a transaction affecting that property; it does not bar its admission for a collateral purpose where otherwise admissible. The proviso added by the 1929 amendment permits admission of an unregistered document as evidence of a collateral transaction not requiring registration. The Court relied on Sambayya v. Gangayya for the test of whether the personal obligation and the property charge are distinct, severable transactions: the personal obligation must exist independently and must not be contingent or conditional on a breach of an obligation concerning the property.

rule.if: award_enforcement_proceeding and independent_personal_obligation and charge_created_to_secure_obligation and charge_unregistered and personal_obligation_severable_from_charge

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: A party sought to have an arbitration award filed and enforced, and the opposing party contested its admissibility.
predicates.independent_personal_obligation: The award directed a party to pay a sum of money as a personal debt that existed independently of any right against property.
predicates.charge_created_to_secure_obligation: The award added a charge over immovable property as security for the payment obligation.
predicates.charge_unregistered: The charge created by the award was not registered.
predicates.personal_obligation_severable_from_charg: The payment obligation could operate independently, while the charge only added a right to proceed against property if payment was not made.

issues.definition: In an award-enforcement proceeding, an unregistered property charge does not exclude proof of a personal payment obligation when that obligation exists independently and can be severed from the charge.

issues.legal_issue: A lawful and severable part of an award may be enforced even when another severable part cannot lawfully be given effect.
material_facts: The award contained a personal direction to pay money and a separate charge over immovable property securing that payment.
The charge was not registered and could not affect the property, while the personal obligation could stand independently.
Giving effect to the personal obligation without the charge did not prejudice the payors and freed them from the additional liability against the property.
issues.conclusion: The personal-obligation part of the award could be given effect despite the invalid, severable charge part; doing so did not impermissibly modify the award.
issues.legal_principle: A separable portion of an award that is bad does not prevent the remainder, if good, from being maintained. The Court relied on Mst. Amir Begam v. Badruddin Hussain and applied the distinction between a lawful, enforceable part and a severable part that cannot lawfully be given effect.

rule.if: award_enforcement_proceeding and award_has_severable_parts and one_part_cannot_lawfully_be_enforced and remaining_part_is_lawful

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: A party sought to have an arbitration award filed and enforced, and the opposing party contested its admissibility or enforcement.
predicates.award_has_severable_parts: The award contains distinct parts that can operate independently of one another.
predicates.one_part_cannot_lawfully_be_enforced: One distinct part of the award cannot lawfully be given effect.
predicates.remaining_part_is_lawful: The other distinct part is lawful and capable of being given effect on its own.

issues.definition: When an award has distinct parts, the lawful part may be enforced on its own if another part cannot lawfully be enforced and the parts are severable.

issues.legal_issue: An award is not inadmissible for non-payment of stamp duty when the required duty and penalty have been paid and the stamped copy accompanies the original.
material_facts: The arbitrators filed the original award, which was not engrossed on stamp paper, with a true copy engrossed on stamp paper attached to it.
The required stamp duty and penalty had been paid, and their sufficiency was not disputed.
issues.conclusion: The award was admissible in evidence and could not be rejected on the ground that the proper stamp duty and penalty had not been paid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35 of the Stamp Act governs the admissibility of an insufficiently stamped instrument. The Court accepted that an instrument of this kind could be admitted after the proper duty and penalty had been paid, and agreed that the stamped copy attached to the original demonstrated payment in this case.

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: A party sought to have an arbitration award filed and enforced, and the opposing party challenged its admissibility.
predicates.unstamped_original_accompanied_by_stampe: The original award was not engrossed on stamp paper, but a stamped copy was attached to it.
predicates.required_duty_and_penalty_paid: The required stamp duty and penalty for the document had been paid.

issues.definition: In an award-enforcement proceeding, an unstamped original accompanied by a stamped copy is admissible on the stamp ground when the required duty and penalty have been paid.
